turns.prompt_text: I would like to learn UML. I took a course on it in college, and I didn't fully understand it. But I also felt I didn't need it that much at the time. Now I do. I would like to find some learning materials, books, videos, what have you, to learn all about UML. I am probably going to end up designing my own system because I dislike a lot of UML, I recall.
turns.response_html:
It is entirely normal to bounce off UML when first seeing it in an academic setting. Often, courses teach it as an exercise in bureaucratic box-checking rather than as a functional tool for thinking. If your goal is to understand it deeply so you can pick apart its flaws and adapt or design your own streamlined system, approaching it from a pragmatic, engineering-focused perspective is the right move.

Here is a curated list of materials—ranging from concise conceptual books to practical text-to-diagram engines—that will give you a solid foundation without drowning you in academic dogma.

Essential Reading (Books)

  • UML Distilled: A Brief Guide to the Standard Object Modeling Language by Martin Fowler
    • Why read it: This is widely considered the antidote to bloated UML books. Martin Fowler strips away 90% of the standard's unnecessary weight and focuses on the 10% that people actually use in the real world. It’s short, pragmatic, and heavily focused on why diagrams matter rather than rote memorization of syntax.
  • Applying UML and Patterns: An Introduction to Object-Oriented Analysis and Design and Iterative Development by Craig Larman
    • Why read it: If you want to understand object-oriented design principles alongside UML, Larman’s book is the gold standard. It teaches you how design models map to code logic, which helps bridge the gap between "drawing pictures" and "building systems."
  • The Elements of UML 2.0 Style by Scott W. Ambler
    • Why read it: This book explicitly covers best practices and stylistic conventions. If you want to redesign or critique how diagrams are constructed, seeing what constitutes "clean" versus "messy" notation is invaluable.

Practical & Visual Web Resources

  • Lucidchart’s Unified Modeling Language (UML) Tutorial
    • An clean, highly readable web guide that breaks down structural diagrams (classes, components) and behavioral diagrams (sequence, activity) with clear visual examples. It is great for a rapid refresher on what each symbol is supposed to mean.
  • Sparx Systems UML Tutorial
    • A more technical, exhaustive overview hosted by Enterprise Architect that walks through the official semantics of the 13 core UML diagram types defined by the Object Management Group (OMG). Use this as a reference manual when you want to know the strict specification before breaking it.

Code-Driven Modeling (For System Designers)

Since you mentioned designing your own system and likely dislike dragging and dropping shapes in heavyweight GUI tools, you may find Text-to-Diagram tools much closer to your workflow. Writing architecture in plain text allows you to version-control your models alongside your code.

  • PlantUML: Lets you write class, sequence, use case, and activity diagrams using a simple, human-readable plain text syntax, rendering them instantly. It exposes how rigid or flexible diagram syntax can be when automated.
  • Mermaid.js: Similar to PlantUML, natively integrated into many markdown environments. It’s fantastic for quickly sketching out flowcharts, sequence interactions, and state transitions without getting bogged down in graphical layouts.

Strategy for Designing Your Own System

As you review these materials with an eye toward rolling your own variant, keep a running log of your friction points:

  1. What is redundant? (e.g., Do you actually need separate notation for aggregation vs. composition, or does a simple directional dependency suffice?)
  2. Where does standard UML obscure rather than clarify? (e.g., Complex state machines or overly verbose deployment diagrams).
  3. What automation do you need? Tailor your custom notation so it can either be parsed programmatically or generated straight from code metadata.
